strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant empirical phenomenon: SAM generally improves test accuracy while increasing measured membership leakage across five datasets.

The evaluation includes strong online and offline LiRA/RMIA attacks, AUC, and low-FPR metrics. For example, CIFAR-100 online LiRA TPR at 0.1% FPR increases from 27.0% to 31.0%, while test accuracy improves from 67.7% to 69.1%.
Additional architectures and ASAM/GSAM experiments broaden the empirical evidence. The memorization and influence analyses offer an interesting hypothesis about the role of atypical examples.
weaknesses: The theoretical model is not established as a model of SAM. Section 5 substitutes minimum-G-norm interpolation with G = I + ηΣ, using population covariance, without deriving this geometry from SAM. For empirical squared loss, every exact interpolant has the same worst-case loss within a fixed Euclidean perturbation ball, since the residual after perturbation is simply Xε. Moreover, replacing Σ with the empirical Hessian in the proposed geometry leaves the minimum-norm interpolant unchanged. Thus, the variance result concerns a different regularizer and does not establish SAM's claimed implicit bias.

The likelihood-ratio guarantee has substantive errors. Lemma 11 requires v_in > v_out for the optimal test to accept large absolute scores, but Assumption 1 does not establish this ordering. Corollary 5 is false as stated: with member variance 1, reducing nonmember variance from 4 to 2 decreases optimal distinguishability. Lemmas 9–10 also combine an unconditional member distribution with a conditional nonmember distribution without justifying the resulting Gaussian likelihood ratio. Furthermore, variance contraction over fresh inputs does not establish contraction across shadow models for a fixed query, as needed for the claimed LiRA connection.

Theorem 4 does not follow from minority alignment alone. The proof treats F_B as common across models, although B = -y⟨w1,ν⟩ changes with their majority-feature weights. The alignment quantity A is also scale dependent, whereas classification is invariant under positive rescaling. Additionally, Lemma 14 infers vanishing test-noise contributions from normalized near-orthogonality without establishing the necessary bound on ||w3||. These gaps undermine the claimed generalization ordering.

The central subgroup comparison is insufficiently controlled. Appendix H.2 constructs different SAM and SGD buckets; only 1,116 examples overlap between their approximately 1,900-example first buckets. Figure 4 needs an explicit comparison on identical test subsets before its differences can be attributed to improved atypical-example performance. Equation 5 is also undefined for all-zero influences and can produce invalid probabilities with signed influences; assigning zero-influence cases maximal typicality does not resolve the general normalization issue.

The proposed causal explanation remains speculative. Intermediate memorization scores and selected tiger/bicycle examples do not establish that the relevant samples represent rare, generalizable subclasses rather than other forms of difficulty or noise. Selecting the most influential examples further limits population-level conclusions. The paper does not quantitatively connect atypicality, prediction-variance changes, and per-example attack success, so claims of identifying the root mechanism exceed the evidence.

Experimental uncertainty and reproducibility are incomplete. Although shadow-attack results average over ten splits, dispersion estimates are absent, which matters for the smaller tabular differences. The comparison against published SGD memorization scores does not document sufficiently matched training and score-estimation protocols. SAM-radius sensitivity and controls for training fit or calibration would also help distinguish an optimizer-specific privacy effect from configuration-dependent behavior.
